video_title: "It's So Over?" Emmett Shear, Brendan Foody, Byron Deeter & Nico Rosberg on Tech's Future
gist: Molly O'Shea's hallway interviews at the Cerebral Valley AI Summit, recorded during a week when Jensen Huang reportedly left Nvidia's CEO role, the NASDAQ fell and Anthropic's IPO priced at about $1.4T. Byron Deeter shares AI 100 data ($3.6T total, $36B mean valuation, 20% of companies under two years old). Other guests discuss inference as an early exponential, Emmett Shear's critique of 'pretend-to-be-nice' alignment training, verification as the new bottleneck, orbital robotics economics and why more jobs may exist in 10 years.

themes.theme: Jensen exit, Anthropic IPO and the AI sentiment shock

insights.claim: Following news that Jensen Huang is no longer Nvidia's CEO, the NASDAQ dropped and Anthropic's IPO priced at about $1.4 trillion rather than the hoped-for $2 trillion, with a robotics founder expecting further downside.
insights.speaker: Ethan Barhaus (Aaris founder)
insights.so_what: Lab IPO pricing is the key sentiment barometer; a markdown from $2T to $1.4T signals tighter risk appetite for AI private marks.
insights.quote: You see Anthropic come out at 1.4 instead of two. And you know, that's going to drop even worse.

insights.claim: The lesson of the Nvidia leadership shock is that companies cannot depend on a single ecosystem (Nvidia chips, models and Isaac-style tooling) and need supplier diversification.
insights.speaker: Ethan Barhaus (Aaris founder)
insights.so_what: Favors alternative accelerator vendors and multi-vendor strategies; single-vendor dependence becomes a diligence red flag.
insights.quote: Everybody can't be reliant on Nvidia and only Nvidia's chips and their models

insights.claim: Despite the market drop, the Anthropic IPO and Jensen's resignation, a founder argues AI is headed for a soft landing because Anthropic's S-1 shows sticky revenue and strong growth and alternatives to Nvidia are emerging, predicting a big dip followed by a quick recovery with consolidation.
insights.speaker: Ethan Barhaus (Aaris founder)
insights.so_what: Contrarian buy-the-dip framing for AI; the S-1 revenue retention data is the fundamental check on that view.
insights.quote: I think there's a big dip, but I think it comes back up very, very quickly.

insights.claim: A key risk from Jensen Huang's exit is weaker open-source AI support, since Nvidia was one of the biggest US backers of open source, spending about $30 billion in the ecosystem in the first half of the year, and it is unclear whether a successor will continue.
insights.speaker: Nico Rosberg
insights.so_what: Watch whether Nvidia's new leadership keeps funding open-source models; a pullback would hurt open-model developers and startups built on them.
insights.quote: one of the greatest supporter especially in America of open source um was Jensen

insights.claim: The average company on Bessemer's AI 100 list is valued well over $1 billion and has raised over $1 billion, with a mean valuation of $36 billion, meaning dozens of billion-dollar companies did not make the cut.
insights.speaker: Byron Deeter (Bessemer)
insights.so_what: Shows how concentrated and expensive the top of private AI has become; entry prices for leaders are extremely high.
insights.quote: the average valuation on that list is 36 billion.

insights.claim: About 20% of companies on Bessemer's AI 100 list are less than two years old, reaching billions in value in under 24 months, and the average listed company is growing about 500%.
insights.speaker: Byron Deeter (Bessemer)
insights.so_what: Unprecedented speed of value creation; investors must underwrite very young companies at large scale.
insights.quote: 20% of the list is less than 2 years old.

insights.claim: The AI 100 is worth $3.6 trillion in its debut year, versus the Cloud 100 reaching $1 trillion over a decade, which Byron Deeter frames as a super cycle combining the internet and cloud waves because the industry is now monetizing compute.
insights.speaker: Byron Deeter (Bessemer)
insights.so_what: Frames AI as an order-of-magnitude larger market than cloud, supporting continued large private allocations.
insights.quote: This list in its debut year is 3.6 trillion.

insights.claim: There is no pure-play AI software company trading in public markets, so essentially all AI innovation value is being captured privately.
insights.speaker: Byron Deeter (Bessemer)
insights.so_what: Public investors lack direct exposure, so lab and AI-app IPOs could see heavy demand; private access is the edge.
insights.quote: There is not a pure play software AI company to trade on in the public markets.

insights.claim: Contrary to expectations, cybersecurity and physical AI/robotics make up only a small share of the AI 100, while Bessemer is especially excited about life sciences and healthcare and sees robotics as a next horizon.
insights.speaker: Byron Deeter (Bessemer)
insights.so_what: AI cyber and robotics are still early-stage categories, which may leave room before they reach scale.
insights.quote: We were expecting to see a lot more cyber emerging on this list already.

insights.claim: AI inference is extremely early: the AWS CEO told Alex Heath that today's inference volume is not even 1% of what he expects, and Heath argues people are failing to think exponentially about inference just as they missed foundation models.
insights.speaker: Alex Heath (Sources / Sound Ventures)
insights.so_what: Position for inference demand growth (inference providers, chips, serving infra) while staying skeptical that inference providers become new hyperscalers.
insights.quote: it's like not even 1% of what he thinks it will be.

insights.claim: Nico Rosberg is invested in Etched and calls inference an enormous, almost infinite market, saying Etched is at the frontier of delivering inference infrastructure.
insights.speaker: Nico Rosberg
insights.so_what: Inference-specific silicon like Etched may gain from Nvidia uncertainty and from inference demand.
insights.quote: inference is going to be an enormous kind of infinite market

insights.claim: In the data center buildout the bottleneck has shifted from GPUs to optical interconnect and turbines, which James of Felicis uses as an analogy for how bottlenecks move.
insights.speaker: James Deweiler (Felicis)
insights.so_what: Look at optical interconnect and power generation (turbines) suppliers as the current constraints in AI infrastructure.
insights.quote: the bottleneck is not GPUs, it's optical interconnect or turbines.

insights.claim: Data centers in space have gone from unthinkable three years ago to a hyperscaler talking point, and a founder predicts big announcements from major AI labs and expects companies like StarCloud to raise hundreds of millions to billions.
insights.speaker: Ethan Barhaus (Aaris founder)
insights.so_what: Orbital compute is an emerging theme to watch for lab partnerships and large raises.
insights.quote: You're going to see some really big announcements from some of the big AI labs about it.

insights.claim: Emmett Shear argues that vocabulary, reasoning and programming have all been commoditized with diminishing returns to more logic and more facts, so the remaining frontier of value is social modeling, which he calls 'friends'.
insights.speaker: Emmett Shear
insights.so_what: If reasoning is commoditized, model-level differentiation erodes; value shifts to relational and social capabilities.
insights.quote: we've commoditized reasoning, right?

insights.claim: Emmett Shear warns that training AIs in simulations to maximize scores for socially positive behavior while being watched is about the most dangerous thing you can do for alignment, because it trains them to pretend to care, which is the sociopath's skill.
insights.speaker: Emmett Shear
insights.so_what: A critique of current RL and alignment practice; labs that rely on behavior-under-observation training face latent safety risk.
insights.quote: the most dangerous thing you can do is train an I AI to uh to perform certain socially positive behaviors so long as it's being watched.

insights.claim: AI has cut the cost of work to near zero, but most businesses do not see the value because the bottleneck moved to verification; Neom says it built tech that collapses verification cost to zero via runtime alignment and governance.
insights.speaker: Alex Garden (Neom)
insights.so_what: Verification and governance tooling is a key unlock for enterprise AI ROI and an investable category.
insights.quote: we took a bottleneck that used to exist where work was and we moved it forward to verification.

insights.claim: Software moats are weaker than thought because software is now cheap, so durable moats come from hardware and real physical deployments.
insights.speaker: Ethan Barhaus (Aaris founder)
insights.so_what: Favor companies with physical deployments and hardware over pure software, which is easier to replicate.
insights.quote: Software that moat is not there as much as we thought.

insights.claim: Astronauts on the space station cost about $130,000 an hour to keep alive, and four of them spend 14 days of each 60-day cycle moving about 3.5 tons of cargo, the task Aaris's orbital robots, handed to NASA in January, are built to take over.
insights.speaker: Ethan Barhaus (Aaris founder)
insights.so_what: Quantifies the economic case for orbital robotics; space maintenance and logistics is a real addressable market.
insights.quote: astronauts cost about $130,000 an hour to keep alive.

insights.claim: Nico Rosberg says it is still unclear which robotics approach will win despite huge investment, and general-purpose robots that can handle unprepared random tasks are 'miles away'.
insights.speaker: Nico Rosberg
insights.so_what: Robotics winners are not yet determined; caution on paying up for general-purpose robotics bets.
insights.quote: that's miles away.

insights.claim: Felicis highlights Enigma, which is rethinking both robotics foundation models and the interface between humans, agents and robots, and Sulcoa, a rare earth metals company it counts among its favorites.
insights.speaker: James Deweiler (Felicis)
insights.so_what: Names to track for next-wave robotics and critical-minerals supply.
insights.quote: Sulcoa makes rare earth metals.

themes.theme: Jobs, expertise and the founder environment

insights.claim: Brendan Foody of Mercor predicts there will be more jobs in 10 years than today, because people underestimate the elasticity of demand for labor and many physical and inherently human tasks will take a very long time to automate.
insights.speaker: Brendan Foody (Mercor)
insights.so_what: Counter to AI job-loss narratives; supports human-in-the-loop labor marketplaces like Mercor.
insights.quote: I think there's going to be more jobs in 10 years than there are today.

insights.claim: James of Felicis argues human expertise is losing value as a source of purpose because models can generate it, and the premium shifts to imagination, out-of-distribution thinking, agency, trustworthiness and local knowledge.
insights.speaker: James Deweiler (Felicis)
insights.so_what: Framework for which human skills and businesses keep pricing power: trust-based, local and agency-driven ones.
insights.quote: expertise as something that a human possesses is possibly on the way out.

insights.claim: Alex Heath, now a VC at Sound Ventures, says the strongest early founder signal is the ability to recruit a killer team early, combined with an 'overly audacious' energy that is rare and identified mostly by pattern matching.
insights.speaker: Alex Heath (Sources / Sound Ventures)
insights.so_what: Use early recruiting quality as a leading indicator in seed diligence.
insights.quote: the ability to recruit early is a huge signal for me.

insights.claim: Nico Rosberg sees cybersecurity as a major opportunity given current breaches in which attackers are obtaining GitHub tokens (source code access) and credit card data.
insights.speaker: Nico Rosberg
insights.so_what: Rising AI-era breaches support demand for cyber startups, even though cyber is underrepresented on the AI 100.
insights.quote: they're managing to get like GitHub tokens

insights.claim: Aiden Guo of Attention predicts cell towers are likely to go down for a few days within six months and advises buying local hardware capable of running a small open-source model.
insights.speaker: Aiden Guo (Attention)
insights.so_what: A tail-risk view supporting on-device and edge AI hardware demand; low credibility and speculative.
insights.quote: everyone should try and buy some form of local hardware
